I leant upon a coppice gate When Frost was spectre-grey, And Winter's dregs made desolate The weakening eye of day. The land's sharp features seemed to be The Century's corpse outleant, His crypt the cloudy canopy, The wind his death-lament. The ancient pulse of germ and birth Was shrunken hard and dry, And every spirit upon earth Seemed fervourless as I. outputs.L1:
I leaned upon a coppice gate  
When Frost was spectre-grey,  
And Winter’s dregs made desolate  
The weakening eye of day.  
The tangled bine-stems scored the sky  
Like strings of broken lyres,  
And all mankind that haunted nigh  
Had sought their household fires.  

The land’s sharp features seemed to form  
The Century’s outstretched corpse,  
His crypt the cloudy canopy,  
The wind his death-lament.  
The ancient pulse of germ and birth  
Was shrunken, hard, and dry,  
And every spirit upon the earth  
Seemed as devoid of fervour as I.  

At once, a voice arose among  
The bleak twigs overhead,  
In a full-hearted evensong  
Of boundless joy;  
An aged thrush—frail, gaunt, and small,  
With blast-beruffled plume—  
Had chosen thus to fling his soul  
Upon the growing gloom.  

So little cause for carolling  
Of such ecstatic sound  
Was written in terrestrial things,  
Afar or near around,  
That I could only think there trembled through  
His happy goodnight air  
Some blessed Hope, of which he knew  
And I remained unaware.
outputs.L2:
I rested against the gate of a thicket while the frost cast a ghostly grey over everything, and the final bleak remnants of winter dimmed the fading daylight. Twisted climbing stems cut across the sky like the snapped strings of ruined harps, while everyone who had lingered nearby had withdrawn to the warmth of home.

The harsh outlines of the landscape appeared like the sprawled body of the dying century. The cloud-covered sky formed its tomb, and the wind sounded like a funeral dirge. The age-old force that brings forth growth and life seemed hardened, withered, and drained; every living soul appeared as empty of passion as I felt.

Suddenly, from the bare branches above, a song burst out—an evening hymn overflowing with limitless happiness. It came from an old thrush, a small, thin, fragile bird whose feathers had been ruffled by the wind. As the darkness deepened, it chose to pour its entire spirit into its music.

Nothing visible anywhere, either close by or in the distance, seemed to justify such an intensely joyful song. I could only imagine that the bird’s cheerful farewell to the day carried some sacred promise of hope—one known to the thrush but hidden from me.
outputs.L3:
At the close of the nineteenth century, the speaker surveys a bleak winter landscape covered in frost. The surroundings appear empty, cold, and lifeless, while the weakening light suggests that both the day and the century are drawing to an end. The desolate scene resembles a corpse, reinforcing ideas of exhaustion, decay, and death. It also reflects the speaker’s own emotional state, as he feels isolated and unable to imagine a hopeful future.

The silence is suddenly broken by the song of an aged and frail thrush. Despite its physical weakness and the harsh conditions around it, the bird sings with extraordinary joy and passion. Its ecstatic music contrasts sharply with the gloom of the landscape and the apparent lifelessness of the natural world. The speaker cannot identify any visible reason for such happiness. He therefore concludes that the thrush may possess knowledge of some hidden and blessed hope—a source of renewal or meaning that exists beyond his own understanding.
outputs.L4:
In Thomas Hardy’s “The Darkling Thrush,” the speaker surveys a bleak winter landscape at the close of the nineteenth century. Frost appears “spectre-grey,” the weakening sun resembles a “dregs” of day, and tangled branches stretch across the sky like the strings of broken lyres. These images make the natural world seem lifeless, silent, and spiritually exhausted. The land itself becomes “the Century’s corpse outleant,” transforming the end of an era into a scene of death and burial. This desolation also reflects the speaker’s inner condition: he can find no source of vitality either in the landscape or within himself, while the people who might provide companionship have withdrawn into their homes.

The sudden song of an aged thrush therefore creates a striking contrast. Frail, weather-beaten, and apparently as close to death as the surrounding world, the bird nevertheless pours out an “evensong” of ecstatic joy. Nothing visible in the landscape explains its “full-hearted” celebration. The speaker does not simply adopt the thrush’s optimism, but he begins to wonder whether the bird possesses knowledge unavailable to him—some “blessed Hope” hidden from human perception. The poem consequently ends with uncertainty rather than confident consolation. Yet that uncertainty is meaningful: amid apparent death and despair, the thrush’s song opens the possibility that renewal, faith, or sustaining hope may exist beyond what present circumstances allow the speaker to see.
outputs.L5:
### When Frost Arrives

When frost settles quietly across the fields, the world seems to pause. Grass glitters beneath the pale morning light, and bare branches shine like delicate glass. Each frozen breath reminds us that winter has arrived, bringing silence, beauty, and the promise of warmer days to come.
